name: Replit AI
description: Browser-native cloud development platform where the 'Repl' (a cloud REPL / project) is the workspace and Replit Agent runs inside that same environment. The Agent has full access to the Repl's filesystem, terminal, package manager, database, and deployment pipeline, turning natural-language prompts into running apps via a plan-edit-run-test-deploy loop. User identity is tied to a Replit account; projects have persistent state with automatic checkpoints, and the workspace supports Google-Docs-style real-time multiplayer editing.
user_identity_model: Users authenticate with a Replit account (email/password or social login) to access the workspace; identity is required and account-scoped. Enterprise Organizations support SAML SSO via an external IdP plus SCIM for automated user provisioning/deprovisioning and group/role sync (Enterprise plan only), with SOC 2 certification and role-based access control. Separately, 'Replit Auth' is an end-user auth service for apps the Agent builds (OpenID/email/profile scopes, sign-in with a Replit account) — distinct from the developer's own login to the platform.
multi_user_collaboration: Strong native multiplayer: a Repl can be shared and edited by multiple users simultaneously with real-time Google-Docs-style co-editing, and the Agent is part of that shared workspace — all participants see the Agent's responses and actions. In practice one person typically drives the Agent to avoid conflicting instructions. Caveat: the Agent has no file-lock awareness, so it can read/write a file a teammate is mid-edit. Enterprise Organizations add team isolation, RBAC, SSO/SCIM, private deployments, and admin controls; deactivating a user retains (does not delete or transfer) their Repls.
workspace_definition: The workspace is a 'Repl' — a cloud-hosted project bundling code, a Linux runtime, terminal, package manager (Nix-based environment), optional Postgres database, and deployment config, all account-scoped and accessible from the browser (and mobile). It is a virtual, account-scoped project entity rather than a local filesystem path; it is not inherently 1:1 with a git repo (git is optional inside it). State lives server-side in Replit's cloud compute+storage fabric, so the workspace persists across sessions and devices without local setup.
workspace_session_binding: Agent conversations/sessions run inside a specific Repl and are scoped to that Repl. Checkpoints capture not only code but the AI conversation context, so the Agent thread is bound to (and persisted with) the workspace. Because the Repl is collaborative, multiple users can be active in the same workspace concurrently, but the Agent is generally treated as a single shared conversational thread per Repl rather than independent per-user Agent sessions. [uncertain] Whether truly independent simultaneous Agent sessions per workspace are supported is not clearly documented.
context_scoping: Context is predominantly workspace (Repl) level: the Agent has access to the full Repl environment — filesystem, terminal, packages, database, deployment — plus the Agent conversation history within that Repl. Workspace-level instruction context is carried in a replit.md / project-config file and the .replit config. [uncertain] Cross-Repl global memory or account-level shared instructions are not prominently documented; context appears rebuilt per workspace. Users can also teach the Agent specialized knowledge via pre-built or custom 'skills.'
config_file_instruction_precedence: The .replit file is the protected workspace configuration (run command, environment, etc.) and replit.nix defines the Nix environment. A replit.md-style project file conveys project conventions/instructions to the Agent. Critically, the Agent is sandboxed at the OS/process level so it is deterministically blocked from modifying key files — git history, the .replit config, and Agent state files — even though advanced users can still edit them via Shell/git. [uncertain] A formal multi-file precedence cascade and explicit size caps for instruction files are not clearly documented.
source_corpus_grounding_scope: Not applicable — Replit is a coding/app-building IDE, not a research-assistant product. The Agent's grounding is the Repl's own codebase, environment, and connected database, augmented by optional Web Search and 100+ service integrations, rather than a curated document/source corpus (NotebookLM/Perplexity Space style).
persistence_mechanism: Hybrid cloud persistence. Replit runs a compute+storage 'snapshot engine' using a manifest model: checkpoint copies the current manifest under a new name and restore swaps to a prior manifest version, giving fast isolated forks of code state. Application/user data persistence is provided by an integrated serverless Postgres (Neon), which the Agent auto-provisions when an app needs data and which supports git-like database branching. App History / checkpoints therefore persist both code state (via Replit's storage fabric) and database state (via Neon branches) together. Storage is effectively snapshot/branch-oriented rather than a single append-only log.
session_history: Checkpoints are automatically created by the Agent at major milestones; each is a complete snapshot of the Repl state — code, workspace contents, AI conversation context, project/dependency configuration, environment tool settings, and optionally database contents. App History provides a global timeline across all Agent sessions and deployments that users can scroll through, roll back, and even roll forward, and can time-travel to a prior state to interact with the running app without affecting the main app/database. History is browsable via the history view in the Agent tab. [uncertain] Underlying storage record format and retention/export specifics for the conversation log are not fully documented.
memory_layering: Short-term/thread state is the Agent's in-Repl conversation context, persisted as part of each checkpoint. Durable, user-authored guidance comes from project config/instruction files (.replit, replit.md) and reusable 'skills' the user installs or authors. [uncertain] There is no prominently documented automatically-generated, evolving long-term memory store akin to Windsurf/Claude auto-memory; cross-thread durability is achieved primarily through checkpointed conversation context and the persistent workspace itself rather than a separate distilled memory layer.
search_retrieval_history: App History exposes a navigable timeline of states across all Agent sessions and deployments for a given Repl, so prior states are retrievable (rollback/roll-forward/time-travel) without manual copy-paste. [uncertain] This is timeline navigation rather than documented full-text or semantic search over past sessions, and cross-Repl/account-wide history search is not clearly documented.
lifecycle_ttl_cleanup: Persistent-by-default rather than ephemeral: Repls and their checkpoint/App-History timeline persist server-side across sessions and devices until the user deletes them; rollbacks are non-destructive (roll-forward remains possible). The snapshot engine's isolated forks let the Agent experiment in a reversible sandbox and discard failed attempts via rollback. Deactivating an Org user retains their Repls (no auto-deletion/transfer). [uncertain] No published TTL/auto-expiry for inactive Repls or a hard-delete-vs-archive retention policy for checkpoints.
sandbox_isolation_model: The Agent operates inside the Repl's cloud Linux environment (Nix-based, fully isolated reproducible environment) with network/web access for installing packages, calling APIs, and deploying. A key safety layer is OS/process-level sandboxing of the Agent specifically: it is deterministically blocked from editing protected files (git history, .replit, Agent state), preventing AI non-determinism from destroying critical state — stronger than prompt-only guardrails. The snapshot engine provides isolated, reversible forks of both code and database so the Agent can try risky changes safely, with automatic dev/prod database separation introduced after early incidents.
snapshot_state_restore: Yes, this is a core feature. Checkpoints/App History capture full environment state — workspace contents, project configuration (dependencies, packages, runtime config), dev-tool settings, and optionally database contents — and can be restored independently to time-travel the entire environment, not just conversation history. Database state restore is powered by Neon branching so code and schema/data are rolled back together to a consistent prior point. Restoring returns the whole Repl (compute env + data) to the snapshot's exact state.
cloud_local_handoff: Primarily cloud-only: the Repl, Agent, environment, and deployment all live in Replit's cloud and are accessed via browser or mobile; there is no first-class self-hosting/local-execution mode for the Agent. Portability is via standard exports (download/clone the code, connect git) rather than moving a live stateful session between cloud and local.
parallelism_subagent_fanout: [uncertain] The Agent presents largely as a single coordinated builder per Repl (planner + code editor + execution + deploy), with supporting capabilities like background tasks and Kanban-style planning. The snapshot engine enables isolated forks for safe experimentation, but a documented multi-parallel-agent or many-worktree fan-out (Cursor/Devin-style N parallel agents) is not prominent. Multiplayer concurrency is human-driven co-editing within one shared workspace rather than parallel autonomous Agent instances.
trigger_surface: Primary surface is the browser-based Repl workspace (Agent chat panel). Also available via the Replit mobile app. Sessions are initiated by the user prompting the Agent in natural language inside the workspace; collaborators in the same Repl share that Agent surface. [uncertain] GitHub-issue/PR-mention triggers, a dedicated CLI-driven Agent trigger, and cron/webhook session creation are not prominently documented as Agent entry points (background tasks exist within a Repl, but external event triggers are unclear).
implementation_stack: Identity: Replit accounts (email/password + social login), with Enterprise SAML SSO + SCIM and RBAC; 'Replit Auth' (OpenID scopes) for end-user app auth. Workspace runtime: Nix-based reproducible Linux environments per Repl. State/persistence: a custom compute+storage 'snapshot engine' using a manifest model for fast isolated, reversible forks of code/workspace state; integrated serverless Postgres via Neon (with git-like branching) for application data and as the substrate for App History's data time-travel; Agent-added apps get an ORM layer with schema validation and input sanitization. Safety: OS/process-level sandboxing that deterministically protects git history, .replit, and Agent state files. Agent intelligence: 'Dynamic Intelligence,' Web Search, and 100+ integrations (OpenAI, Stripe, Discord, etc.). [uncertain] Exact databases used for platform-side session/metadata storage beyond Neon are not fully disclosed.
applicability_to_labmate: Replit is the 'workspace-as-persistent-cloud-environment' end of the spectrum and offers several lessons for Labmate. (1) Identity: account-scoped identity with optional enterprise SSO/SCIM maps to Labmate keying everything on a stable user identity (Discord connector) with room to layer org/team scoping later. (2) Workspace model: the Repl as a virtual, account-scoped, persistent entity (not a disk path) directly validates Labmate's workspace_id-as-DB-entity approach (MongoDB long-term session docs) where compute is detachable from the durable workspace record. (3) Checkpointing: Replit's manifest-based snapshot engine that captures code + conversation context + DB state together is a strong analog to LangGraph thread_id checkpointing plus Redis active state — Labmate should consider snapshotting conversational/thread state alongside any mutable artifact state so rollback restores a consistent point. (4) Data time-travel via Neon branching is likely overkill for Labmate, but the principle (code/state and data must be versioned together to restore a coherent prior session) should inform what Redis Streams + MongoDB jointly capture. (5) Multiplayer caveat: the Agent's lack of file-lock awareness in a shared workspace is a direct warning — if multiple users (or a user + agent) act on one Labmate workspace concurrently, define a locking/turn-taking or last-writer-wins policy explicitly. (6) Safety pattern: deterministically protecting critical state files at the process level (not via prompt) is a transferable guardrail — Labmate should hard-guard durable session/identity records from agent mutation rather than relying on instructions. (7) Trigger surface: Replit is workspace-UI-initiated (vs Jules's event/issue trigger), so Labmate's Discord-message entry point sits closer to Jules; Replit mainly reinforces the persistent-workspace and history-retrieval API design.
